alignments.note: Privative adjective rendered by a periphrasis: *free from* spells the alpha-privative and *the love of money* glosses the φιλάργυρ- lexeme, so rule 84's head on the meaning-bearing noun applies and the unit heads on *love* rather than on *free*. Rule 91 then chooses *love* over *money* inside that phrase: the corpus spends *silver* on ἀργυρ- in all four of its units and *money* in none, so *money* is no gloss of the stem and could be chosen only as the phrase's formal complement, which rule 17 forbids, while the φιλ- family heads the love-word wherever the English glosses that element separately. The Greek clause is verbless and the predicate is adjectival, so the supplied copula *Be* is a rule 53 helper on the predicate rather than on the subject, and the supplied subject pronoun *ye* rides with it here for the same reason: rule 27 forbids splitting a helper from what licenses it, and 1PE.3.14 and 1PE.4.14 both give `μακάριοι` → *blessed are ye* the supplied copula and subject pronoun together on the predicate adjective, unhedged. The alternative of aligning *ye* to `τρόπος` is stated at s003 and rejected there.

Article governing the expressed noun τρόπος. The ASV writes no determiner and no possessive for that noun — it recasts ὁ τρόπος as the bare subject pronoun *ye* — so nothing is left for the article and rule 23 decides it. Giving *ye* to the article instead is the competing reading; I took the noun as its carrier because rule 96 records that no corpus unit aligns an article to a supplied English subject pronoun it does not itself realize, and rule 89's address-word case is scoped to a vocative, which this nominative is not.

The ASV recasts `ὁ τρόπος` as a second-person subject and writes no English for the noun itself: *ye* is second person where `τρόπος` is a third-person noun meaning *manner of life*, so it realizes no part of this lexeme and rule 17's requirement that a head most directly realize the source lexeme is not met. The noun is therefore `unrepresented` under rule 23 and the supplied *ye* folds into the predicate's own supplied frame at s001 under rules 7, 27 and 68, as 1PE.3.14 and 1PE.4.14 give `μακάριοι` → *blessed are ye* both supplied words together on the predicate adjective. Aligning `τρόπος` to *ye* is the competing reading and remains defensible, since rule 68's first configuration is scoped to a clause expressing no subject at all whereas this clause does express one; I rejected it because the corpus aligns no common noun anywhere to a bare English subject pronoun, and 1KI.17.22 `עַל קִרְבּוֹ` → *into him* shows this project's habit of emptying the lexical noun and keeping the pronoun on the token that realizes it. Giving *ye* to the article instead is ruled out by rule 96, which records that no unit aligns an article to a supplied subject pronoun it does not itself realize, and by rule 89's address-word case being scoped to a vocative, which this nominative is not.
Participle rendered by the bare predicate adjective *content*.

Substantival article before a participle, taking the supplied nominal expression *such things*. Rule 49's mid-rule clause is what licenses this and it names the participle in terms — where the article's complement is an adjective or a participle nothing else can carry the determiner, so a supplied nominal is the article's own. Rule 32 governs only the other half: the participle keeps its own clause and the relativizer *as*, and the article does not absorb it. Rule 102 heads the unit on the supplied nominal *things* rather than on the determiner-like *such*, the corpus heading all fifty-three such units on the nominal and none on the determiner; JHN.18.4, JHN.16.13, PHP.1.10, TIT.1.5 and 2CO.4.18 are the precedent line, each an article before a participle taking *the things* whole. The dative's case preposition *with* rides with the article under rule 21, no Greek preposition being expressed for rule 36 to give it to, as JAS.2.5 says of the same configuration. The competing reading is 1PE.2.7's, which gives the same ASV idiom whole to the verb — `ἀπιστοῦσιν` → *for such as disbelieve* — and remains defensible; it does not carry here because that participle is anarthrous and no article stood to take the determiner, and because *such* standing in an article's determiner slot is otherwise unattested.
The participle carries the finite relative clause the ASV writes for it; the relativizer *as* and the supplied subject *ye* are rule 7 and 9 helpers, and rule 17 heads on the lexical verb *have*.
Perfect indicative with its auxiliary; rule 9 heads on the lexical verb *said*.
Emphatic οὐ μή. Rule 33 keeps *in no wise* whole on the particle pair, headed on οὐ and on the English *no*, and forbids splitting the phrase across the two particles or emptying either.
Aorist subjunctive with the ASV's supplied subject and future auxiliary; rule 9 heads on the lexical verb *fail*. The negation belongs to the οὐ μή unit, not here.

Coordinating negative conjunction → *neither*. Rules 41 and 59 do not empty it: what follows is the οὐ μή pair carrying its own English negation phrase, not a negative indefinite absorbing this word's negation.

Second emphatic οὐ μή, kept whole as *in any wise* under rule 33. The ASV writes *any* rather than *no* here because the preceding *neither* already carries the clause's negative word, so rule 33's *headed on the English no where there is one* has no *no* to take and the head falls on the quantifier *any*. REV.18.14 is the corpus's on-point precedent for an `οὐ μή` whose English carries no *no*: rendered by the bare *at all*, it heads on the quantifier *all* and not on the preposition. The head of an `οὐ μή` English frame sits on the negator or quantifier slot in all fifteen multiword corpus units and never on *in*, *at*, or the frame noun *wise*, which realizes no part of the negation — JHN.21.1's `οὕτως` → *on this wise* heads on *wise* only because a manner adverb is what *wise* glosses. Rule 24 confirms it: this unit and the verse's first `οὐ μή` are then one analysis rather than two.

Aorist subjunctive with supplied subject and auxiliary, discontinuous under rule 15; rule 9 heads on the lexical verb *forsake*. SBLGNT.HEB.13.5.v002 is underdetermined and the projected base reading is among those the English permits, so rule 12 leaves it as projected and no rule 97 note is owed.

review_notes: Every s### and t### is partitioned exactly once: 18 source tokens across 16 units, 34 target tokens with none repeated or dropped.

The main open question is where the ASV's *ye* sits. I gave it to τρόπος and left ὁ `unrepresented`; the competing reading, article-as-subject-pronoun, is named in the s002 note. A reference comparison may report ὁ as a disagreement.

Both οὐ μή pairs are single `noncompositional` units under rule 33. The second is headed on *any* because the ASV's *neither* has already taken the clause's negative word, leaving no *no* for rule 33's default head.
s001 heads on *love* per rule 84's privative-plus-noun line, not on *free*; the supplied copula *Be* rides with the adjectival predicate under rule 53 rather than with the subject.
